title: IF YOU DISAGREE ABOUT MARY, ARE YOU REALLY DISAGREEING ABOUT JESUS?
paragraphs: IF YOU DISAGREE ABOUT MARY, ARE YOU REALLY DISAGREEING ABOUT JESUS?
The ancient controversy that divided Christians, the Greek word that changes the conversation, and the biblical truth we must never sacrifice while defending what we believe.
There is something heartbreaking about watching two people who genuinely love Jesus Christ begin treating each other like enemies because they disagree about His mother.
One says, “Mary is the Mother of God.”
The other responds, “God has no mother.”
One hears that response and wonders whether the other person truly believes Jesus is God.
The other hears the title Mother of God and worries that Mary is being elevated to a place Scripture reserves for the Lord alone.

And suddenly, what began as a conversation about a woman who humbly surrendered her life to God's will becomes a battlefield of accusations, wounded relationships, and questions about who is truly Christian.
But here is the question that should stop both sides before another argument begins.
What if two Christians can disagree about Mary's role while wholeheartedly confessing the same eternal, divine Savior?
And what if, beneath some of those disagreements, there are also genuine theological questions that deserve more than a dismissive answer?
Because not every disagreement about Mary is a denial of Christ.
But neither is every disagreement merely a matter of personal preference.
Some distinctions matter enormously.
And the most important one takes us back to a young Jewish woman, an angelic announcement, and a Child whose birth would change human history forever.
Before Mary was the subject of theological debates, she was a young woman facing an extraordinary calling.
Before Christians argued about her titles, she was confronted with a promise that seemed humanly impossible.
Before generations painted her image, composed hymns about her, or debated the meaning of her obedience, she was listening to an angel tell her that she would conceive a Son.
Luke records the angel's announcement:
“The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God.” — Luke 1:35, KJV
Think about what Mary was being told.
Her future was about to change.
Her reputation could be questioned.
Her engagement to Joseph would face an unimaginable test.
She could not control how people would interpret her pregnancy.
And yet, in the middle of uncertainty, she responded with surrender.
“Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word.” — Luke 1:38, KJV
There is something profoundly beautiful about that response.
Mary did not possess all the answers.
She did not know every hardship awaiting her.
But she trusted the God who had spoken.
And perhaps that is where this conversation should begin.
Not with hostility.
Not with caricatures.
Not with the assumption that every Christian who uses a different title for Mary must secretly believe in a different Jesus.
But with Scripture.
Because Mary herself directs our attention toward the One who saves.
In Luke 1:46–47, she declares:
“My soul doth magnify the Lord, And my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour.”
Notice those words.
God my Saviour.
Mary's own testimony is not that she stands independently above the need for divine grace.
Her song is a celebration of God's mercy, faithfulness, and saving work.

Christians have disagreed about how Mary's need for a Savior relates to doctrines such as the Immaculate Conception. Catholics understand that doctrine as God's grace preserving Mary from original sin through the merits of Christ; Protestants generally reject that interpretation.
But the biblical declaration itself remains unmistakable.
Mary rejoices in God her Savior.
And every faithful Christian understanding of Mary must ultimately lead us back to Him.
Now we come to the word that has caused centuries of controversy.
Theotokos.
It is a Greek word written:
Θεοτόκος
It is commonly translated as “God-bearer” or “Mother of God.”
For some Christians, that title expresses a precious truth about Jesus.
For others, it sounds dangerously close to suggesting that Mary somehow originated God's divine existence.
But those two meanings are not the same.
And understanding the difference is essential.
The Greek word Theotokos was used in early Christian theological discussions and became especially important during the fifth-century controversy surrounding Nestorius and Cyril of Alexandria.
At the Council of Ephesus in AD 431, the title was affirmed in the context of defending the unity of Jesus Christ's person.
Why?
Because the question was not whether Mary created God.
She did not.
The question was whether the One born of Mary was truly God incarnate.
John 1:1 declares:
“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”
And John 1:14 continues:
“And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us.”
The Greek of John 1:14 begins:
Καὶ ὁ λόγος σὰρξ ἐγένετο
Kaì ho lógos sàrx egéneto.
“And the Word became flesh.”
That sentence is breathtaking.
The eternal Word did not begin existing in Bethlehem.
The divine Son did not come into existence when Mary conceived Him.
The One who was with God and was God entered human history by taking on genuine human nature.
He was not merely a remarkable human being who later became divine.
He was not a human person temporarily occupied by God.
He was the eternal Son who truly became man.
This is why the historical title Theotokos mattered so deeply to its defenders.
They were not trying to make Mary the source of divinity.
They were defending the identity of her Son.
The person Mary bore was Jesus Christ, the eternal Son of God incarnate.
His divine nature had no beginning.
His human life in the womb began through the miraculous conception described in Scripture.
The distinction is crucial.
Mary is the mother of Jesus according to His humanity. She is not the origin of His deity.
Yet Jesus is not two separate persons, one human and one divine.
He is one person, truly God and truly man.
The Council of Chalcedon in AD 451 would articulate this confession with extraordinary care: Christ is acknowledged in two natures, without confusion, change, division, or separation.
That is the heart of historic orthodox Christology.
And it means something important for this conversation.
A Christian who rejects the title Mother of God because they believe it misleadingly suggests that Mary created God's divine nature is not necessarily rejecting Christ's divinity.
They may be objecting to what they understand the title to imply.

But a Christian who rejects the title because they believe Jesus was merely human, or that the person born of Mary was not truly the eternal Son incarnate, is rejecting a foundational Christian confession.
Those are profoundly different positions.
One may be a dispute about language and its theological implications.
The other concerns the identity of Jesus Himself.
And we should never confuse the two.
Consider another biblical expression.
In Luke 1:43, Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, says to Mary:
“And whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?”
The Greek reads:
καὶ πόθεν μοι τοῦτο ἵνα ἔλθῃ ἡ μήτηρ τοῦ κυρίου μου πρὸς ἐμέ;
Kaì póthen moi toûto hína élthē hē mḗtēr toû kyríou mou pròs emé?
The key expression is:
ἡ μήτηρ τοῦ κυρίου μου
Hē mḗtēr toû kyríou mou.
“The mother of my Lord.”
The Greek word Kyrios means “Lord.” Its precise force depends on context, but Luke's account unmistakably presents the child as uniquely significant in God's saving purpose.
Elizabeth honors Mary because of the extraordinary identity of the Child she carries.
That does not mean Luke is teaching that Mary is the creator of God.
Nor does it mean Elizabeth is treating Mary as divine.
The honor is inseparable from the Lord whom Mary bears.
This is where thoughtful Christians can begin to understand one another, even when they remain divided.
Catholic and Eastern Orthodox Christians commonly regard Theotokos as an important safeguard of the incarnation.
Many Protestants also affirm the title when it is properly defined.
Other Protestants prefer “mother of Jesus” or “mother of Christ,” fearing that Mother of God can be misunderstood or used to support devotional practices they do not believe Scripture authorizes.
The important question is not simply which words someone uses.
It is what they actually confess about Christ.
Do they believe Jesus is eternally divine?
Do they believe He truly became human?
Do they believe He is one person, not two?
Do they confess Him as Lord and Savior?
Those questions reach the center of Christian faith.
But we must go further.
Because the disagreements about Mary do not end with a title.
Christians also disagree about her perpetual virginity, her sinlessness, her assumption into heaven, her intercessory role, and the proper forms of honor shown to her.
These are not all the same kind of disagreement.
And pretending that they are would be intellectually dishonest.

Catholic teaching affirms Mary's Immaculate Conception and bodily Assumption as doctrines of faith. Eastern Orthodox Christians honor her as all-holy and celebrate her Dormition, while expressing aspects of Marian theology differently from Roman Catholicism.
Most Protestants do not accept the Immaculate Conception or Assumption as doctrines established by Scripture.

Catholics and Orthodox also distinguish the veneration given to Mary from the worship owed to God alone. Many Protestants nevertheless believe that some Marian prayers and devotional practices lack biblical warrant or risk obscuring Christ's unique mediatorship.
These disagreements are real.
They cannot all be resolved by saying that everyone simply means the same thing.
They involve different understandings of Scripture, apostolic tradition, doctrinal authority, prayer, and the communion of saints.
But here is what must not be lost.
Disagreeing about those doctrines does not automatically mean someone denies that Jesus Christ is God.
A Christian can affirm the full deity of Christ while rejecting the Assumption of Mary.
A Christian can affirm the incarnation while disagreeing with Catholic teaching about Marian intercession.
And a Christian can affirm historic orthodox Christology while honoring Mary as Theotokos.
We must evaluate each claim carefully rather than condemning an entire person through association.
And perhaps this is where the argument becomes painfully personal.
Because sometimes we are no longer defending Scripture.
We are defending our pride.
We have become so determined to win the debate that we have forgotten the command to speak the truth in love.
Ephesians 4:15 calls believers to speak “the truth in love.”
Not truth without love.
Not love without truth.
Both.
Have you ever been in a conversation where someone misunderstood what you believed, but instead of asking you to explain, they immediately condemned you?
Have you ever tried to defend Christ and ended up speaking with a harshness that looked nothing like Him?
Have you ever shared a verse not because you wanted someone to understand the Word of God, but because you wanted to silence them?
That is an uncomfortable question.
Especially for those of us who know Scripture well enough to quote it, but sometimes struggle to live it.
The Bible does not command us to abandon doctrinal discernment.
It does command us to examine the manner in which we exercise it.
Paul writes in 2 Timothy 2:24–25:
Gentleness is not theological weakness.
Patience is not compromise.
And refusing to misrepresent another Christian's beliefs is not surrendering biblical conviction.
It is honesty.
It is humility.
It is obedience.
But we must also confront another danger.
In our desire to avoid conflict, we may be tempted to say that doctrine does not matter at all.
That would be equally mistaken.
The identity of Jesus Christ is not negotiable.
John's Gospel does not present Jesus as merely one spiritual teacher among many.
Thomas addresses the risen Christ:
“My Lord and my God.” — John 20:28
The Greek confession is:
ὁ κύριός μου καὶ ὁ θεός μου
Ho kýriós mou kaì ho theós mou.
“My Lord and my God.”
Jesus does not reject Thomas's confession.
The narrative presents it as the climactic recognition of who the risen Christ truly is.
And Paul writes in Colossians 2:9:
The incarnation is not a decorative doctrine.
It is central to the Gospel.
If Jesus were merely a created being, He would not be the eternal Word who became flesh.
If He were not truly human, He would not have genuinely entered our condition.
The New Testament proclaims both His full divinity and His real humanity.
Hebrews 2:14 speaks of His participation in flesh and blood.
Hebrews 4:15 declares that He was tempted as we are, yet without sin.
He experienced hunger.
He grew tired.
He wept.
He suffered.
He bled.
He died.
And He rose again.
This is the Savior Mary carried.
This is the Savior Joseph was commanded to name Jesus.
This is the Savior who came to redeem sinners.
And when we argue about Mary, we must never allow the argument to eclipse the very Son who makes her place in salvation history meaningful.
Remember the wedding at Cana.
The wine had run out.
Mary brought the need to Jesus.
And in John 2:5, she told the servants:
“Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it.”
There is remarkable wisdom in those words.
Whatever Christians conclude about the broader theological significance of Mary, this recorded instruction points away from self-sufficiency and toward obedience to Christ.
Do what He says.
Not merely what your religious culture says.
Not merely what your favorite online teacher says.
Not merely what your denominational instincts demand.
Listen to Jesus.
Search the Scriptures.
Test what you hear.
And follow the Lord.
That does not erase centuries of serious theological disagreement.
But it does establish the direction in which every Christian's devotion must ultimately move.
Toward Christ.
Always toward Christ.
Now consider something even more moving.
At the cross, Mary stood near the suffering of her Son.
John 19:25 places her among those standing by the cross of Jesus.
Imagine the sorrow.
The Child she had carried was now suffering a brutal execution.
The One whose birth had been announced with such extraordinary promise was being publicly humiliated.
The hands she had once held were pierced.
The Son she loved was dying.
We must be careful not to invent Mary's unrecorded thoughts.
Scripture does not tell us everything she felt.
But it does tell us she was there.
And any parent who has watched a child suffer knows that there are kinds of grief language can barely contain.
Yet the Gospel does not end at the cross.
The crucified Jesus rose from the dead.
And the salvation accomplished through His death and resurrection is the hope of every sinner who turns to Him in faith.
Not because Mary possessed divine power.
Not because the disciples were morally flawless.
Not because the church was free from human weakness.
But because Jesus Christ is Lord.
The same Mary who was present in the Gospel accounts is later mentioned among the believers gathered in prayer in Acts 1:14.
She is there with the disciples, participating in the life of the early believing community.
And that detail matters.
The woman who received the angel's announcement did not replace the risen Lord.
She belonged to the community gathered in His name.
What a powerful reminder that even those uniquely privileged in God's redemptive story remain dependent upon His grace.
And now the question returns to us.
What are we actually defending when we argue?
Are we defending the truth of Christ's incarnation?
Are we carefully examining doctrines that we believe Scripture does or does not support?
Or are we defending a religious identity so fiercely that we have forgotten the people standing in front of us?
Some of those people are carrying wounds we cannot see.
Some have been taught to fear anything associated with another Christian tradition.
Some have been accused of idolatry without anyone first asking what they actually believe.
Others have been accused of denying Christ's divinity simply because they refused a particular Marian title.
Some have experienced genuine spiritual confusion from devotional practices they could not reconcile with Scripture.
Others have experienced the pain of hearing deeply held beliefs caricatured rather than accurately represented.
None of those experiences proves a doctrine true.
Truth is not established by how deeply a teaching comforts us.
But those experiences should remind us that theological arguments involve real human beings.
People for whom Christ died.
People who need truth.
People who also need patience.
And perhaps some of us need to repent.
Not necessarily because our doctrinal convictions are wrong.
But because our attitudes have become sinful.
We have confused cruelty with courage.
Sarcasm with discernment.
Suspicion with faithfulness.
And victory in an argument with faithfulness to Jesus.
The Gospel calls us to something better.
It calls us to truth without dishonesty.
Conviction without arrogance.
Correction without contempt.
Love without doctrinal indifference.
And humility without surrendering what God has revealed.
This is especially important when discussing the unique mediatorship of Christ.
First Timothy 2:5 declares:
“For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus.”
That verse must be taken seriously.
Catholic and Orthodox Christians understand the intercessory prayers of saints as subordinate to Christ's unique mediation, not as a replacement for it.
Many Protestants argue that addressing prayers to departed saints is not taught or warranted by Scripture and prefer prayer directed to God through Christ.
Those are substantive disagreements deserving careful biblical and theological examination.

But both the Catholic or Orthodox Christian who affirms Christ as the sole source of saving mediation and the Protestant who insists upon direct access to the Father through Christ can confess Jesus as fully divine.
Their disagreement over Marian intercession does not, by itself, settle the question of whether either one believes in the deity of Christ.
At the same time, a claim that Mary is herself divine, the source of Christ's deity, or an independent redeemer equal to Jesus would contradict the biblical understanding of God and salvation.
Precision matters.
Because false accusations do not become righteous merely because we believe we are protecting the truth.
And neither does false teaching become harmless simply because it is expressed with sincerity.
We need Scripture.
We need discernment.
We need grace.
We need the courage to say, “I believe this teaching is wrong,” without automatically declaring, “Therefore, you do not believe Jesus is God.”
And we need the humility to ask, “What do you mean?” before deciding what another person believes.
There is a reason the apostle Paul urged believers to be “kindly affectioned one to another with brotherly love; in honour preferring one another” in Romans 12:10.
The Christian life is not a contest to see who can humiliate the most people with Bible verses.
It is a life transformed by the mercy of God.
And that mercy should change how we speak.
Especially when we disagree.
Perhaps you are reading this as a Catholic who has always honored Mary and has felt misunderstood by Protestant friends.
Perhaps you are Protestant and have been troubled by Marian doctrines you believe go beyond Scripture.
Perhaps you are Orthodox and see in the ancient title Theotokos a confession of the mystery of the incarnation.
Or perhaps you are a new believer who simply wants to know whether loving Jesus means you must accept every claim anyone makes about His mother.
Hear this carefully.
Your salvation is not secured by winning an argument about Mary.
The Gospel announces salvation through Jesus Christ.
Ephesians 2:8–9 declares:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
The foundation of our hope is not the perfection of our theological vocabulary.
It is the crucified and risen Savior.
That does not make correct doctrine unimportant.
It means that doctrine must serve the truth about Him rather than become an instrument of spiritual pride.
The Son of God did not enter human history so that we could turn His mother into a weapon against one another.
He came to save sinners.
He came to reconcile us to God.
He came to call us to repentance and faith.
He came to bring the dead to life.
And this is where our Gospel Warrior message becomes deeply personal.
Think about Mary and Joseph.
Before the miracle was widely understood, Mary's pregnancy placed them in a situation that could be interpreted as scandalous.
Matthew 1:19 tells us Joseph initially considered putting her away privately.
But God intervened through an angelic message.
Joseph learned that the Child had been conceived through the Holy Spirit.
And in Matthew 1:21, he was told:
“And she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins.”
There it is.
The reason for the name.
The purpose of the coming.
The heart of the story.
He shall save His people from their sins.
Not merely from embarrassment.
Not merely from misunderstanding.
Not merely from the opinions of others.
From their sins.
The greatest scandal in the human story is not that people disagreed about Mary.
It is that sinful humanity rejected and crucified the sinless Son of God.
And the wonder of grace is that through His death and resurrection, God accomplished redemption for sinners.
The cross exposes the seriousness of sin.
The resurrection announces Christ's victory over death.
And the Gospel invites the guilty, the ashamed, the proud, the wounded, and the spiritually exhausted to come to Him.
That includes the religious debater who has forgotten how to love.
The churchgoer who knows theological terms but has never truly surrendered.
The believer who has been wounded by careless accusations.
The person who has spent years defending a tradition but rarely opening the Scriptures.
And the person who has used religious disagreements as an excuse to avoid confronting the claims of Jesus.
Because at some point, the question becomes intensely personal.
Not simply, “What do you believe about Mary?”
But, “Who is Jesus Christ to you?”
Is He merely a subject you debate?
A religious figure you admire?
A name attached to your upbringing?
Or is He the Lord before whom you bow?
The Savior whose mercy you need?
The risen King whose Word you desire to obey?
Romans 10:9 declares that salvation is connected with confessing Jesus as Lord and believing that God raised Him from the dead.
And John 20:31 explains the purpose of John's Gospel:
“But these are written, that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God; and that believing ye might have life through his name.”
Life through His name.
Not through our ability to defeat another Christian in a comment section.
Not through our religious superiority.
Through Jesus.
So can Christians disagree about the role of Mary without rejecting the divinity of Christ?
Yes. Absolutely.
But that answer needs its proper boundaries.
Christians may disagree over Marian titles, doctrines, and devotional practices while affirming that Jesus is the eternal Son of God, fully divine and fully human.

However, if a person's understanding of Mary or Jesus actually denies the eternal deity of the Son, divides Christ into separate persons, or rejects His genuine humanity, the disagreement has moved into the foundations of Christology.
We must distinguish between a disagreement over how to express the incarnation and a denial of the incarnation itself.
We must also distinguish between recognizing another person's confession of Christ and agreeing with every doctrine that person holds.
Recognizing that someone affirms Jesus' deity does not require us to accept their entire theology.
And rejecting a Marian doctrine does not automatically mean rejecting Jesus.
That is the distinction too many arguments fail to make.
And it is a distinction worth remembering the next time someone posts a provocative statement about Mary.
Before you type your response, ask whether you have understood what the person means.
Before you accuse, examine the evidence.
Before you condemn, remember your own need for mercy.
Before you defend a doctrine, make sure you are defending what Scripture actually teaches.
And before you claim to speak for Jesus, consider whether your words reflect the character of the Lord you proclaim.
Maybe the next conversation will not end in agreement.
It may still end with genuine theological differences.
But perhaps it can end with something that has become painfully rare.
Truth spoken honestly.
Convictions expressed clearly.
Questions asked sincerely.
And two people who disagree refusing to treat one another as less than human.
That would not settle every theological controversy.
But it would be a meaningful act of Christian faithfulness.
And if this article has exposed something in your own heart, do not rush past it.
Maybe you have judged someone before understanding them.
Maybe you have been afraid to ask difficult questions.
Maybe you have confused inherited assumptions with biblical convictions.
Maybe you have allowed theological debates to consume more of your attention than prayer, repentance, and obedience.
Bring that before the Lord.
You do not need to pretend you have every answer.
You do need to be willing to follow the truth wherever Scripture leads.
And if you have never truly entrusted yourself to Jesus Christ, do not let another religious argument distract you from the Savior.
Turn from sin.
Believe the Gospel.
Call upon the Lord.
He is not merely the subject of an ancient controversy.
He is the living Christ.
The One who died for sinners and rose again.
The One whose grace can transform a human life.
The One who can take what seemed permanently ruined and write a story of redemption.
If this message challenged you, I want to hear something more meaningful than which side of an argument you belong to.
Your testimony, your questions, and even your respectful disagreement may help someone else who has been silently struggling.

Invite someone who is struggling in faith, someone who has drifted away from church, or even someone who does not yet believe. They do not have to agree with every conclusion before they can begin examining the claims of Jesus.
There is also something important I want to share with those who believe this ministry is worth sustaining.
Gospel Warrior exists to proclaim Christ, encourage repentance, help believers grow in Scripture, and remind wounded people that the grace of God is greater than the ruins of their past.
But continuing and expanding that mission takes real resources.
Researching and preparing biblical teaching, producing discipleship materials, maintaining resources, and reaching more people all require time, labor, and financial support.
Not because God measures your love for Him by whether you support this particular ministry.
And certainly not because anyone can purchase God's favor.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not arise from reluctance or compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
Think of it as a voluntary, recurring ministry offering that helps sustain and expand the resources made available to others.
Someone you may never meet could encounter a message that encourages them to open the Bible again.
Someone overwhelmed by guilt could be reminded of the forgiveness offered through Christ.
Someone trapped in religious confusion could begin asking better questions about the Gospel.
We cannot promise what God will do through every article.
But we can faithfully labor to make biblical truth accessible, understandable, and available.
These free resources are part of the heart of the ministry.
And monthly supporters help make ongoing work possible.
Because the greatest treasure we want anyone to receive is not merchandise.
It is a deeper knowledge of Jesus Christ through His Word.
Keep reading.
Keep learning.
Keep opening your Bible.
Keep praying.
Keep sharing the truth.
We are not building a community where people must pay to belong.
We want to build a community where people are continually pointed toward Christ.
Because the Gospel is not a product to be purchased.
It is good news to be proclaimed.
And the Savior at the center of that Gospel is worthy of far more than an online argument.
He is worthy of our worship.
Our repentance.
Our obedience.
Our love.
Our lives.
So the next time you hear someone say, “Mary is the Mother of God,” or someone else respond, “God has no mother,” remember that a single phrase may conceal a much deeper question.
Ask what they mean.
Ask what they believe about Jesus.
Return to Scripture.
Study the historical context.
And refuse to let pride become more important than truth.
Mary's significance in the biblical story is inseparable from the identity and mission of her Son.
The eternal Word became flesh.
The promised Savior was born.
The sinless Christ died for sinners.
The risen Lord conquered death.
And everyone who comes to Him in faith finds their ultimate hope not in the perfection of their religious arguments, but in the grace and saving work of Jesus Christ.
One day, our arguments will fall silent.
Our reputations will no longer impress anyone.
Our denominational labels will not be able to cleanse our sins.
And the only Savior sufficient to reconcile us to God will still be Jesus Christ.
Do not become so consumed with arguing about the woman who carried the Savior that you forget to surrender your life to the Savior she carried.
